scenes.animation: Zippy writes a letter to the Municipal Commissioner that begins 'Hey bro! Wassup?' with a smiley. The letter flies to a stern office, where the Commissioner, a cartoon file with glasses, drops it straight into a dustbin labelled 'Informal'.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Why did my complaint land in the dustbin?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Because a formal letter needs a formal format and a formal tone. Let's build one, block by block.

scenes.animation: A blank letter sheet. Blocks drop in one at a time from top to bottom, each labelled: '1. Sender's address', '2. Date', '3. Receiver's designation and address', '4. Subject', '5. Salutation: Sir / Madam', '6. Body', '7. Yours faithfully / Yours sincerely', '8. Name (and signature)'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Start with your address, then the date. Next, the receiver's designation and address.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Then a clear subject line, and the salutation, Sir or Madam.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: After the body, close with yours faithfully or yours sincerely, followed by your name.

scenes.animation: The body block zooms in and splits into three coloured slices: 'Para 1: who you are and why you write', 'Para 2: details, facts, reasons', 'Para 3: request / action expected, thanks'. A word counter in the corner ticks up to '100-120 words'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Write the body in three short paragraphs. First, introduce yourself and state the purpose.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Second, give the details, facts and reasons. Third, say what action you expect, and thank the reader.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The word limit is one hundred to one hundred and twenty words.

scenes.animation: A marks meter fills in four coloured segments: 'Format 1', 'Content 2', 'Organisation of ideas 1', 'Accuracy 1'. A small note under Format reads 'Half mark lost if one or two parts are missing'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The letter carries five marks. One for format, two for content, one for organisation of ideas, and one for accuracy.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In the CBSE marking scheme, missing one or two parts of the format costs half a mark, and missing more costs the whole mark.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So the address and date are free marks!

scenes.animation: A mini practice card: 'Which is wrong in a formal letter? (a) Subject line (b) Yours faithfully (c) Dear Buddy (d) Date'. '(c) Dear Buddy' is stamped with a red cross. A 'BOARD TIP' sticker reads 'Choose 1 of 2 questions; no slang, no SMS language'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Quick check. Which does not belong in a formal letter: subject line, yours faithfully, dear buddy, or the date?

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Dear buddy. Obviously.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Board tip: you get a choice of one out of two letters. Pick the one where you have more ideas, and never use slang or short forms like pls.

scenes.animation: Recap board with a neat letter mascot wearing a tie. Points appear: '1. Address, date, receiver, subject, salutation, body, close, name', '2. Three paragraphs, 100-120 words', '3. Format 1 + Content 2 + Organisation 1 + Accuracy 1'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: follow the full format, from your address to your name.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: write three short paragraphs in one hundred to one hundred and twenty words.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: marks go to format, content, organisation and accuracy.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Dear Commissioner, I sincerely apologise for bro.

name: Formal Letter: Letter to the Editor

scenes.animation: A street full of stray plastic bags that fly around like ghosts. Zippy shouts at them, but nobody hears. Neo hands him a newspaper whose front page grows into a huge loudspeaker.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: The whole colony is drowning in plastic, and nobody listens to me!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Then write to the editor of a newspaper. Thousands of people, and the officials, will read it.

scenes.animation: The letter format builds up with the receiver block highlighted: 'The Editor, The Times of India, New Delhi'. Then the subject line types itself: 'Subject: Need for a ban on single-use plastic in our locality'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A letter to the editor is written to raise a public issue, not a personal problem.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Address it to the Editor, with the newspaper's name and city. Keep the subject short and specific.

scenes.animation: A three-slice body appears. Slice 1 shows the opening line 'Through the columns of your esteemed newspaper, I wish to draw the attention of the authorities to...'. Slice 2 shows icons of blocked drains and a cow eating plastic. Slice 3 shows icons of cloth bags and a municipal van.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Open with the classic line: through the columns of your esteemed newspaper, I wish to draw the attention of the authorities to the problem.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In the second paragraph, give the causes and effects, like blocked drains and animals eating plastic.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In the third, suggest solutions and appeal to the authorities to act.

scenes.animation: Zippy writes 'This is the WORST colony ever!!!' in angry red letters; Neo gently replaces it with 'The situation needs urgent attention.' A tone dial swings from 'angry' to 'firm and polite'.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Can I say it's the worst colony in the world?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Be firm but polite. Say the situation needs urgent attention. Examiners reward a formal tone.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Also, avoid naming or blaming individuals. Focus on the issue and on what the authorities can do.

scenes.animation: A practice card: 'Write a letter to the editor about the rising noise pollution during festivals.' Three content bullets appear: 'effects on the sick, elderly and students', 'loudspeakers beyond permitted hours', 'suggest time limits and strict checks'. A 'BOARD TIP' sticker reads 'Content marks = points covered from the question'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Practice. Plan a letter to the editor about noise pollution during festivals.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Problem: loudspeakers late at night. Effects: the sick, the elderly and students suffer. Solution: time limits and strict checks.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Well planned. Board tip: content marks come from covering every point the question gives you, so tick them off as you write.

scenes.animation: Recap board with the newspaper-loudspeaker. Points appear: '1. Public issue, addressed to The Editor', '2. Open: Through the columns of your esteemed newspaper...', '3. Problem → effects → solutions; firm, polite tone'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: a letter to the editor raises a public issue and is addressed to the Editor.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: begin with, through the columns of your esteemed newspaper.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: describe the problem, its effects and solutions, in a firm, polite tone.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Dear Editor, the plastic bags have been warned.

scenes.animation: Zippy unboxes a brand-new mixer grinder. He presses the switch; the jar spins off, flies around the kitchen and lands in a pot of dal. Zippy stands dripping with dal.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Two days old, and my mixer grinder is already a flying saucer!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Time for a letter of complaint. Clear facts, a firm tone, and a specific demand.

scenes.animation: The letter builds with the receiver block highlighted: 'The Manager, Sharma Electronics, Karol Bagh, New Delhi'. The subject types itself: 'Subject: Complaint regarding a defective mixer grinder'. A bill with 'Invoice No. 4521' flashes beside it.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Address the person who can fix the problem, like the manager of the shop or the head of a department.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The subject should say complaint regarding, followed by the problem.

scenes.animation: The body builds in three slices with icons. Slice 1: a calendar and shopping bag 'what, when, where bought'. Slice 2: the flying jar and a crack 'exact defect'. Slice 3: a replacement box and a clock 'demand + time limit'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Paragraph one: what you bought, when and where, with the bill number.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Paragraph two: the exact defect and the trouble it caused.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Paragraph three: what you want, a repair, a replacement or a refund, within a reasonable time.

scenes.animation: Zippy types 'Fix it or I will destroy your shop!!!' The letters catch fire and fall away. Neo's version appears: 'I request you to replace the product at the earliest, failing which I shall be compelled to approach the consumer forum.'

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Can I threaten them a little?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: No threats. Say politely that if the matter is not settled, you will be compelled to approach the consumer forum.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Avoid exaggeration too. State facts the reader can check, like the date of purchase, the bill number and the model.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Model number noted. Dal stains not included.

scenes.animation: A practice card: 'Write a complaint to the Municipal Corporation about irregular garbage collection in your area.' Three points pop up: 'garbage not collected for a week', 'foul smell, flies, disease risk', 'request daily collection and more bins'. A 'BOARD TIP' sticker reads 'Stick to the given situation — do not invent a new one'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Practice. Plan a complaint to the Municipal Corporation about irregular garbage collection.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Not collected for a week. Foul smell, flies and a risk of disease. Please collect daily and add more bins.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Good. Board tip: stay inside the situation the question gives. If the question names you and your address, use exactly those details.

scenes.animation: Recap board with the mixer grinder now fixed and spinning neatly. Points appear: '1. Address the authority who can act', '2. What happened → exact problem → specific demand', '3. Firm, polite; no threats'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: write to the person or authority who can solve the problem.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: give the facts, the exact problem, and a specific demand.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: stay firm and polite, never rude.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: And maybe keep the dal away from the mixer next time.

name: Formal Letter: Letter to Place an Order or Make an Enquiry

scenes.animation: The school library shelves are empty except for one dusty book. A cartoon librarian with round spectacles sighs; Zippy is handed a pen and a letterhead reading 'Librarian, Sunrise Public School'.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: The librarian wants me to order new books. Do I just send a list?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: You send a letter to place an order. It's a business letter, so it must be precise.

scenes.animation: The receiver block lights up: 'The Manager, Modern Book Depot, Daryaganj, New Delhi'. The subject types: 'Subject: Order for books for the school library'. The writer's block shows 'Librarian, Sunrise Public School'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Write as the person in the question, for example, the librarian of your school, and address the manager of the supplier.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The subject should say order for, followed by the items.

scenes.animation: A neat table draws itself inside the letter with columns 'S. No.', 'Title', 'Author', 'Publisher', 'Copies'. Rows fill in. Below, icons appear for 'delivery date', 'discount', 'mode of payment'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In the body, list the items in a small table: title, author or brand, and quantity.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Then mention the delivery date, the discount you expect, and how you will pay.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Add a line asking them to ensure the goods are not damaged.

scenes.animation: A second letter slides in labelled 'Letter of Enquiry'. A question mark bounces on the subject line 'Subject: Enquiry about summer coaching camp'. Bullets appear: 'fees', 'timings', 'facilities', 'last date to join'.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: What if I only want information, like the fees for a cricket camp?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: That's a letter of enquiry. Ask clear questions about fees, timings, facilities and the last date, and request a prospectus.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Keep an enquiry short and polite, since you are asking for help. End with, I shall be grateful for an early reply.

scenes.animation: A practice card: 'Complete: I would like to place an order for the following ____ .' The answer 'items' drops in. A 'BOARD TIP' sticker reads 'Tables are allowed but count toward the word limit; keep the list short'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Mini practice. Finish the opening: I would like to place an order for the following blank.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Items. Or books, if it's for the library.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Right. Board tip: keep the list short and relevant, so that your letter stays near one hundred and twenty words. Don't forget the complimentary close.

scenes.animation: Recap board with a stack of new books flying onto the library shelves. Points appear: '1. Write as the person named; address the supplier', '2. Order: items table + delivery + discount + payment', '3. Enquiry: clear questions, request a prospectus'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: write as the person named in the question, to the right supplier or office.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: an order letter lists the items and states delivery, discount and payment.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: an enquiry letter asks clear questions and requests details.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: The dusty book is finally getting friends.

scenes.animation: A bar graph titled 'Hours spent on screens by teenagers, 2019-2023' stands on stage. Zippy reads every bar aloud like a train announcer: 'Two hours! Three hours! Four hours!' The audience falls asleep.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: I read out every number. Why is everyone asleep?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Because an analytical paragraph isn't a list of numbers. It explains the trend, compares, and draws a conclusion.

scenes.animation: A paragraph template builds up in three colour bands inside one block: 'Introduction: what the graph shows, place, period', 'Body: overall trend, highest, lowest, comparisons with figures', 'Conclusion: what it means'. A crossed-out 'Title' tag floats away.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Write one single paragraph of one hundred to one hundred and twenty words, with no title.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Begin by saying what the graph shows, and for which period. Then describe the overall trend, the highest and lowest points, and compare them with figures.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: End with a conclusion about what the data suggests.

scenes.animation: Arrows zoom along the bars with trend words sticking to them: 'rose steadily', 'peaked at', 'dipped slightly', 'remained constant', 'doubled'. A word bank card slides in.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Use trend words: rose steadily, peaked, fell sharply, remained constant, and doubled.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So instead of two, three, four hours, I say screen time doubled from two hours in 2019 to four hours in 2023!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exactly. That's analysis.

scenes.animation: A marks meter fills: 'Content 2', 'Organisation of ideas 2', 'Accuracy 1'. A warning sign flashes: 'Not a description. Not a summary.'

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: It carries five marks: two for content, two for organisation of ideas, and one for accuracy.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The CBSE marking scheme warns that it should not be just a description or a summary. Examine the data and give inputs.

scenes.animation: A practice card shows a simple chart: 'Cycle sales in a town: 2020 = 500, 2024 = 1,000'. The answer sentence builds: 'Cycle sales doubled from 500 in 2020 to 1,000 in 2024, suggesting a shift towards eco-friendly travel.' A 'BOARD TIP' sticker reads 'Quote the figures accurately; use the past tense for past data'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Practice. Cycle sales in a town were five hundred in 2020 and one thousand in 2024. Write one analytical sentence.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Cycle sales doubled from five hundred in 2020 to one thousand in 2024, suggesting a shift towards eco-friendly travel.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Perfect. Board tip: copy the figures exactly from the chart, and use the past tense for past data.

scenes.animation: Recap board with the bar graph now awake and smiling. Points appear: '1. One paragraph, 100-120 words, no title', '2. Intro → trends and comparisons with figures → conclusion', '3. Content 2 + Organisation 2 + Accuracy 1'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: one paragraph, one hundred to one hundred and twenty words, no title.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: introduce the data, analyse trends with figures, and conclude.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: marks go to content, organisation of ideas, and accuracy.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Screen time doubled. My sleep halved.

scenes.animation: Two maps of the same town side by side, labelled '2005' and '2025'. In 2025 a lake has shrunk, a metro line has appeared and fields have turned into apartment blocks. Zippy plays 'spot the difference' with a magnifying glass.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: It's a spot-the-difference game! Do I just list the changes?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: You list them, group them, and explain what they mean. That's how you analyse a map.

scenes.animation: Changes on the map glow in groups with colour tags: green for 'lost' (fields, part of the lake), blue for 'added' (metro, hospital, mall), grey for 'unchanged' (the old temple, the school).

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Start by saying what the maps show, the place and the years.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Then group the changes: what was added, what was lost, and what stayed the same.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Use location words like to the north of, next to, and replaced by.

scenes.animation: A sentence builds on screen: 'Over two decades, the farmland to the east was replaced by housing, while a metro line now connects the town to the city.' The phrases 'replaced by' and 'while' glow.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Link ideas with words like while, whereas, however and as a result.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: End with a conclusion, for example, the town has become more urban, but at the cost of green spaces.

scenes.animation: A different question appears: two candidate cards for 'Guest speaker for the school debate', each with a few cue points. Zippy weighs them on a cartoon balance scale.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: What if there's no map, just cues?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Then examine the cues closely. If you are asked to choose, like a guest speaker from two candidates, state your choice, show its strengths, and contrast it with the other.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The marking scheme says any view is valid if the reasoning is strong and uses the given evidence.

scenes.animation: A practice card: 'Map cue: 2005 — one bus stop; 2025 — metro station and three bus stops.' The answer builds: 'Public transport expanded considerably, with a metro station added and bus stops rising from one to three.' A 'BOARD TIP' sticker reads 'Use only what is given; no outside facts'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Practice. In 2005 there was one bus stop; in 2025 there is a metro station and three bus stops. One sentence, please.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Public transport expanded considerably, with a metro station added and bus stops rising from one to three.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Excellent. Board tip: use only the information given, and don't invent facts that aren't on the map or in the cues.

scenes.animation: Recap board with both maps pinned side by side. Points appear: '1. Introduce place and period', '2. Group changes: added, lost, unchanged; use location and linking words', '3. Cues: choose, justify with evidence, contrast; conclude'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: introduce what the map or cues show.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: group the changes, using location and linking words.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: with cues, take a view, justify it with evidence, and conclude.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: I'd still vote for keeping the lake.

scenes.animation: Zippy stares at a long passage that grows taller and taller until it towers over him like a skyscraper. He tries to read every word with a tiny torch and gets lost inside.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Four hundred words of someone's opinion! Where do I even start?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Start with the questions, not the passage. Then the passage becomes a treasure map.

scenes.animation: A card explains: 'Section A: Reading — 20 marks'. It splits into 'Discursive passage, 400-450 words, 10 marks' and 'Case-based factual passage, 200-250 words, 10 marks'. The discursive half glows.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Section A has two unseen passages worth twenty marks in all.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The discursive passage is four hundred to four hundred and fifty words long, for ten marks. It presents an argument or a viewpoint on an issue.

scenes.animation: A three-step path lights up: 'Step 1: Read the questions, underline key words', 'Step 2: Skim the passage for the main idea', 'Step 3: Scan to find each answer; mark the paragraph'. Zippy walks the path with a highlighter.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Step one: read the questions and underline the key words.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Step two: skim the passage for its main idea and the writer's tone.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Step three: scan for each answer, and mark the paragraph where you found it.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: For questions on the writer's view, look for signal words like I believe, clearly, however and unfortunately.

scenes.animation: Question types appear as game cards: 'MCQ', 'Complete the sentence', 'Short answer 30-40 words', 'Find the word that means...'. For the vocabulary card, a magnifying glass hovers over 'paragraph 3'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: You'll see multiple choice, sentence completion, short answers of thirty to forty words, and vocabulary.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: They test inference, analysis, interpretation, evaluation and vocabulary.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Inference means reading between the lines, right?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Yes. The answer isn't written directly; you work it out from the clues.

scenes.animation: A mini passage appears: 'Although exams test memory, they rarely measure creativity.' A question: 'The writer's attitude to exams is: (a) admiring (b) critical (c) indifferent (d) angry'. '(b) critical' glows. A 'BOARD TIP' sticker reads 'Answer in your own words; don't copy whole lines'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Practice. Although exams test memory, they rarely measure creativity. Is the writer admiring, critical, indifferent or angry?

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Critical. The word rarely gives it away, but it's not angry.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Correct. Board tip: in short answers, use your own words and keep to the word limit; copying whole lines can cost marks.

scenes.animation: Recap board with the skyscraper passage shrunk to a neat map. Points appear: '1. Discursive: 400-450 words, 10 marks', '2. Questions first → skim → scan', '3. Inference from clues; own words for short answers'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: the discursive passage is four hundred to four hundred and fifty words, for ten marks.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: read the questions first, then skim, then scan.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: infer from clues, and answer in your own words.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Skyscraper defeated.

scenes.animation: A short passage about pens has a pie chart glued to it. Zippy reads the words carefully but covers the chart with his hand, then gets a question wrong and a buzzer honks.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: I read the whole passage. How did I get it wrong?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: You ignored the chart. In a case-based passage, half the facts hide in the visual.

scenes.animation: A card reads 'Case-based factual passage: 200-250 words + visual input (statistical data / chart), 10 marks'. A table, a bar graph and a pie chart orbit the passage like moons.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: This passage is two hundred to two hundred and fifty words long and carries ten marks.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: It comes with a visual input, such as a table, chart or survey data, and presents facts rather than opinions.

scenes.animation: A magnifying glass reads the chart: the title, the axis labels, the units '%' and the legend light up one by one. Then it links a sentence in the passage to a bar with a glowing thread.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Read the chart title, the labels and the units first. Is it a percentage, a number or a year?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Then connect each fact in the passage to the matching part of the chart.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Beware of trap options that are true in real life but not supported by the data. Choose only what the passage and chart actually say.

scenes.animation: A survey table appears: 'Preferred pen among students: Ballpoint 45%, Gel 35%, Fountain 20%'. A question: 'What percentage do not prefer ballpoint?' The calculation '100 - 45 = 55%' writes itself.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Practice. Forty-five percent prefer ballpoint pens, thirty-five percent gel, and twenty percent fountain pens. What percentage do not prefer ballpoint?

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Hundred minus forty-five. Fifty-five percent!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Correct. Gel plus fountain, thirty-five plus twenty, also gives fifty-five. Always double-check.

scenes.animation: Question types appear: 'Identify the trend', 'Complete with a figure from the table', 'Why might...? (inference)', 'Find a word meaning...'. A 'BOARD TIP' sticker reads 'Quote the exact figure with its unit'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Expect questions that ask you to identify a trend, complete a statement with a figure, infer a reason, or find a word.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Board tip: when the answer is a number, write it with its unit, like fifty-five percent, not just fifty-five.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So units are the seatbelts of numbers.

scenes.animation: Recap board with the chart and passage shaking hands. Points appear: '1. 200-250 words + visual, 10 marks', '2. Read title, labels, units; link passage to chart', '3. Check calculations; write figures with units'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: the case-based passage is two hundred to two hundred and fifty words, with a visual, for ten marks.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: read the chart's title, labels and units, and link them to the passage.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: double-check calculations and always write the unit.
